tldr: This paper proposes an innovative parallel elastic actuator (PEA) for humanoid ankles that shares a single gas spring between pitch and roll axes using two cams. It establishes an optimization-based design method to synthesize cam profiles, drastically reducing the 2-DoF torque burden within limited leg packaging space.
hero_caption: Basic structure of the proposed 2-DoF torque compensation mechanism. Rollers placed at both ends of a single central gas spring simultaneously push against orthogonal pitch (upper) and roll (lower) cams, generating simultaneous dual-axis torque compensation from a single elastic element.
overview:
For bipedal humanoid robots to become practical, increasing torque capacity and improving energy efficiency at the ankle joints are unavoidable hurdles. Ankles require massive torque to support body weight and ground reaction forces. However, using low-gear-ratio actuators leads to continuous high current draw during static or low-speed operation, causing severe heat generation and rapid battery drain. On the other hand, while parallel elastic actuators (PEAs) that assist torque with springs are promising, adding independent elastic elements to both pitch and roll degrees of freedom makes the ankle region excessively bulky.

To tackle this, the authors devised a "dual-cam, single-gas-spring architecture." They placed a high-energy-density gas spring at the center, driving two customized upper and lower cams via rollers at both ends. This allows simultaneous torque compensation for both pitch and roll axes within a very compact installation envelope. Furthermore, they formulated a nonlinearly coupled mathematical model capturing how the displacements of both cams interact through the shared spring, and established an optimization framework that automatically synthesizes optimal cam profiles from prescribed torque references.

To validate the concept, the mechanism was integrated into a lower-leg CAD model (leg length 495 mm, weight 3.56 kg) designed for a 1.7 m tall, 65 kg humanoid. Kinematic simulations and finite element analysis (FEA) stress evaluations were conducted under tasks such as static stance loading and sinusoidal torque references. The results demonstrated that even under coupled conditions, the mechanism provides highly accurate compensation against target torques, effectively reduces motor torque requirements, and keeps cam contact stresses well within allowable material limits.
contributions: Proposed an extremely compact dual-cam parallel elastic actuator (PEA) architecture that assists both pitch and roll degrees of freedom simultaneously by sharing a single gas spring.

Derived a unified mathematical model for a 2-DoF torque compensation mechanism that rigorously accounts for the geometric and mechanical coupling of two axes competing for displacement of a single spring.

Established a mathematical optimization framework that automatically calculates customized cam profiles from prescribed target torque profiles while satisfying geometric constraints (curvature radius and stroke).
Completed a full lower-leg CAD design using ball-screw actuation tailored for a 1.7 m humanoid, verifying mechanical feasibility and structural stress safety via FEA and kinematic simulations.

sections.heading: Why springs are needed at the ankle, and why they must be shared
sections.summary: Lowering gear ratios to improve actuator backdrivability leads to severe overheating due to high static current draw. While parallel elastic actuators (PEAs) help mitigate this, packing multiple independent springs into a narrow multi-DoF ankle results in bulky, heavy mechanisms.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to operate effectively in human environments, they simultaneously demand high load capacity, compliance to withstand impacts, and high energy efficiency to sustain long operating times. Recently, the combination of high-torque-density motors and low gear ratios (such as planetary gears) has become mainstream over conventional high-gear-ratio actuators due to superior dynamics and impact resistance.

However, there is a major catch. While lowering the gear ratio reduces mechanical transmission losses, the current required to produce the same load torque spikes significantly. Because electrical Joule heating scales with the square of the current, static posture maintenance or quasi-static tasks like holding heavy payloads cause motors to heat up intensely, drastically cutting into robot runtimes.

To overcome this trade-off, parallel elastic actuators (PEAs), which passively store and release energy, have drawn wide attention. Previous studies have explored placing metal coil springs, rubber bands, or gas springs in parallel with joints to offload motors. Among these, gas springs boast remarkably high energy density and space efficiency.

Yet, a fatal flaw of existing approaches is the requirement of one independent spring element for every single degree of freedom. In an ankle, where pitch (forward/backward) and roll (side-to-side) axes are tightly packed in a spherical workspace, cramming multiple springs and support linkages makes the joint heavily oversized and cumbersome. This study confronts this challenge by introducing an entirely new design philosophy: sharing a single high-density gas spring across two degrees of freedom.

sections.heading: The geometry and coupled mathematical model shaping torque with cams and springs
sections.summary: Starting from contact geometry between a non-circular cam and a roller, the single-axis compensation torque is derived. After selecting the most compact configuration, the model is extended to a 2-DoF coupled system sharing a single gas spring. An optimization problem fitting polynomial cam curves to target torques is also formulated.
sections.details:
This section systematically constructs the geometric principles and mathematical models that allow the proposed mechanism to generate targeted torques.

■ Fundamentals of a Single Torque Compensation Unit (TCU)
First, consider a 2D model where the origin of polar coordinates is set at the joint center of rotation, and a roller contacts a non-circular cam profile $R(\theta)$. The normal vector at the roller-cam contact point does not pass through the origin; instead, it has an eccentric distance (moment arm) $d(\theta)$. The product of the normal contact force $F_c(\theta)$ exerted by the gas spring via the roller and this arm length $d(\theta)$ generates a passive compensation torque $\tau(\theta)$ about the joint. The spring compression $\Delta c(\theta)$ is determined geometrically from the distance change between the origin and roller during rotation, yielding the torque function $\tau(\theta_j)$ relative to joint angle $\theta_j$.

■ Four Configurations and 2-DoF Expansion
Depending on whether the roller is placed on the convex or concave side of the cam, and whether the spring acts on the cam side or the roller side, four structural configurations exist. Analysis revealed that placing the roller on the concave side of the cam with the spring acting on the roller side minimizes material volume, resulting in the lightest and most compact design. Therefore, two such units are connected back-to-back, sandwiching a single gas spring in the middle. The upper roller pushes the pitch cam while the lower roller pushes the roll cam, supporting both orthogonal ankle axes simultaneously. Crucially, because total spring compression is the sum of pitch and roll displacements ($\Delta c_1 + \Delta c_2$), rotating one axis directly alters the assistance torque of the other axis, introducing a nonlinear coupling relationship.

■ Optimization-Based Inverse Cam Design
The design goal is to match output torque to a task-specified reference torque $\tau_{ref}$. The authors express the cam's polar curve $R(\theta)$ as an $m$-th order polynomial (a 4th-order polynomial here) and formulate a nonlinear programming problem with polynomial coefficients as decision variables. The objective is to minimize the sum of squared errors (SSE) against the reference torque. As constraints, in addition to the maximum allowable spring stroke, a strict undercut prevention constraint is enforced: the cam curvature radius $\rho(\theta)$ must strictly exceed the roller radius $r$ to ensure smooth rolling without gouging.

captions.F2: Four possible configurations for the TCU. Configurations with the roller on the concave side of the cam (right) require significantly less cam volume (yellow area) than convex configurations (left), making them ideal for confined ankle spaces.

sections.heading: Leg hardware integration bridging commercial parts and optimization algorithms
sections.summary: An automated workflow was established to select off-the-shelf components, generate cam profiles from target torques, and produce CAD models. The lower leg employs high-efficiency parallel ball screws, achieving a detailed 3.56 kg leg design for a 1.7 m, 65 kg humanoid.
sections.details:
The system design process for translating theoretical models into physical hardware is presented in detail.

■ Cam Design Optimization Workflow
The design pipeline is highly systematic. First, required torque trajectories are extracted from specific tasks, and a commercial component library (specifications of gas springs with various thrusts and strokes, alongside needle roller bearing dimensions) is loaded. Using IPOPT within the CasADi environment, cam parameters are optimized. Resulting contact forces $F_c$ are evaluated by a bearing verification module to confirm that static and dynamic load ratings are satisfied with proper safety margins. Unsuitable candidates are pruned, and the optimal combination of components along with analytical curve data is fed directly into 3D CAD software (PTC Creo) to complete the model.

■ Ball-Screw Drive and Ankle Mechanical Architecture
For the lower-leg drive system, direct parallel ball-screw mechanisms were chosen over traditional harmonic drives or planetary reducers. Two Wuji F50-13 motors (rated torque 1.27 Nm, max speed 6800 rpm) driven by Synapticon SOMANET Circulo 7 drivers are utilized. Embedding the nut inside the rotor to drive the ball screw linearly eliminates auxiliary gearheads, achieving both high efficiency and lightweight packaging. Furthermore, placing heavy actuator components proximally near the knee drastically reduces foot-end inertia, significantly improving dynamic walking characteristics.

The leg measures 495 mm in total length and weighs just 3.56 kg including the foot, matching specifications for a standard adult-sized humanoid (1.7 m, 65 kg). At the ankle center, a Misumi gas spring (GSU70-7-YW or MGSN16-10) is housed inside self-lubricating graphite bushings, achieving friction reduction and space savings without heavy linear guide bearings. Upper and lower cams are bolted for easy removal, allowing torque characteristics to be re-customized for different tasks simply by swapping cam profiles.

captions.F4: Optimization-based design workflow that seamlessly handles task requirements, cam profile generation, commercial bearing strength verification, and CAD synthesis.
captions.F6: Detailed sectional view of the ankle joint interior. Needle rollers and the shared gas spring are vertically packaged with zero wasted space between the opposed upper pitch and lower roll cams.

sections.heading: Simulating torque reduction and verifying cam strength through FEA
sections.summary: Cam shapes were optimized for three target torque scenarios, including standing and loaded tasks, confirming substantial reductions in motor torque. Static FEA of 7075-T6 aluminum alloy cams demonstrated structural safety under peak contact loads.
sections.details:
Simulations were conducted to verify the effectiveness of the optimization framework, the resulting torque relief, and mechanical structural integrity.

■ Torque Compensation Performance
Based on a 65 kg robot with a 200×110 mm foot size and an ankle torque capacity sized for tip-over prevention with a safety factor of 2 (pitch 127 Nm, roll 70 Nm), the mechanism was configured to passively compensate up to 10% (approx. 12.7 Nm pitch, 7 Nm roll). Three target torque sets were evaluated: uncoupled sinusoids where pitch and roll move independently, coupled sinusoids where both axes interact, and a 4 kg static equilibrium payload task tilting the lower leg.

Results showed that in uncoupled tasks, compensated torque matched target torque almost perfectly (with extremely high $R^2$ values). In coupled scenarios where both axes underwent large concurrent motions, sharing a single spring imposed slight fitting limitations, yet motor torque requirements were still drastically slashed. While higher-thrust springs (MGSN) delivered greater torque reduction, lower-thrust springs (GSU) still provided sufficient relief while mitigating stress on components, revealing a clear design trade-off. In the 4 kg payload task, both average and peak torques were markedly lowered compared to bare motor drive, proving direct benefits for motor downsizing and heat reduction.

■ Finite Element Analysis (FEA) Stress Evaluation
Static FEA was performed on cam modules made of aerospace-grade 7075-T6 high-strength aluminum alloy using profiles optimized for the 4 kg payload task. Under peak loads, maximum von Mises stress reached approximately 500 MPa, approaching the material's tensile yield strength. However, relying on Hertzian contact stress theory, the authors explained that this high stress is intensely localized in a tiny subsurface zone directly beneath the contact point, surrounded and constrained triaxially by the bulk elastic material. Because this state prevents macroscopic plastic deformation (denting), sufficient engineering safety margins are maintained.

captions.F7: Torque fitting results for the 4 kg payload support task, comparing target reference torque (Ref) and mechanism compensation torque (Compen). Both pitch (left) and roll (right) axes track accurately bidirectionally.
captions.F8: Comparison of motor torque demand with and without the compensation mechanism. Compared to uncompensated torque demands (No cmp), introducing the proposed mechanism (Compen) substantially reduces net motor torque across the entire motion range.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: Building the physical prototype for walking tests
sections.summary: A dual-cam parallel elastic actuator sharing a single gas spring successfully combines high torque capacity and compactness for 2-DoF humanoid ankles. The next step is fabricating a physical leg prototype from the CAD model to experimentally measure energy efficiency gains during real walking.
sections.details:
This study presented a task-customizable 2-DoF parallel elastic actuator (PEA) aimed at boosting torque capacity and energy efficiency in humanoid ankle joints.

By introducing an unprecedented mechanical structure that assists both pitch and roll axes using an opposed dual-cam setup around a single shared gas spring, the authors formulated rigorous geometric and coupled dynamic models. Furthermore, they established a nonlinear optimization framework to synthesize cam curves directly from target torques, validating mechanical viability through CAD integration, kinematic simulations, and FEA stress evaluations.

Future work focuses on fabricating a physical lower-leg prototype based on the completed CAD model. Through benchtop load testing and various real-world walking and locomotion maneuvers, the team plans to experimentally verify whether theoretical torque compensation is achieved and quantify the percentage improvement in total robot power consumption and energy efficiency.

takeaways: Overturns the conventional assumption that multi-DoF assistance requires multiple springs, proving that a single high-density gas spring sandwiched between two orthogonal cams is remarkably compact and effective.
Formulates the nonlinear 2-axis coupling arising from spring sharing, enabling custom cam synthesis via nonlinear optimization (IPOPT) while satisfying undercut-prevention curvature constraints.

Provides design justification showing that even if contact stresses approach yield strength (around 500 MPa), Hertzian triaxial compressive confinement prevents gross plastic deformation, making lightweight 7075 aluminum viable.
limitations: Because the pitch and roll axes share the exact same spring, their kinematics couple; in fully coupled tasks where both axes move to extreme angles simultaneously, fitting freedom to target torque profiles is more restricted than in multi-spring systems.

Peak cam surface stress reaches near the material yield point (around 500 MPa); while static failure is avoided, long-term durability against contact fatigue wear and fretting during repetitive walking cycles requires real-world physical verification.

Validation is currently limited to CAD kinematic simulations and static FEA; evaluations including machining tolerances, friction losses, and physical measurements of electrical energy savings during walking remain to be conducted.
